prompt: Orders rose 11.1% in the four weeks after a new page went live. The same weeks of the year before, with no new page, rose 10.2%. What does that say about the page?

choices.text: It raised orders by 11.1%
choices.why: Most of that rise happens every year at that point of the calendar.

choices.text: Very little: the calendar explains most of it
choices.why: Right. Before-and-after mixes the calendar into the answer.

choices.text: A 0.9-point rise, the gap between years
choices.why: Two different years differ in many ways; the gap is not a measurement of the page.

choices.text: It did nothing
choices.why: The data cannot say that either; it cannot separate the page from the calendar.

prompt: Why does a random, simultaneous split remove the season, the trend and the holidays from the comparison?

choices.text: They fall on both groups alike
choices.why: Right, so they cancel in the difference.

choices.text: Randomisation smooths the series, much as a moving average of the right length would
choices.why: Nothing is smoothed; both groups see the same calendar.

choices.text: The test is run in a quiet month chosen for the purpose
choices.why: A test can run in any month; what matters is that both groups share it.

choices.text: Statistics corrects for them afterwards
choices.why: No correction is needed; the design does the work.

prompt: In a before-and-after comparison, what is a confounder?

choices.text: A random error in the data
choices.why: Random error is noise; a confounder moves with the time compared.

choices.text: The version shown to the control group
choices.why: That is the control; there is none in a before-and-after.

choices.text: A visitor who sees both versions of the page during the same test, on two different devices
choices.why: That is contamination, lesson 9's subject.

choices.text: Something else that differs between the two times compared
choices.why: Right. The season and the holiday were confounders here.

prompt: Which of these belong in a written hypothesis for a test? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: the exact change
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: the metric that will decide
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: the smallest effect worth shipping
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: the p-value expected
choices.why: A p-value is computed from the data; nobody writes it in advance.

prompt: The hypothesis says the one-step checkout will help 'because the three-step form loses people on phones'. The effect appears on desktops and not on phones. What should the team conclude?

choices.text: The test failed and should be thrown away
choices.why: The metric may still have moved; the explanation is what failed.

choices.text: Nothing; only the primary metric matters
choices.why: It decides shipping, and the reason is what the team learns from.

choices.text: The stated reason did not hold, and that is worth knowing even though the metric moved
choices.why: Right. That is why the reason is written down.

choices.text: Phones need a separate test, with its own hypothesis and its own primary metric
choices.why: Perhaps later; first, the stated reason did not hold.

prompt: Why does this course use a two-sided test even when the team only cares about improvement?

choices.text: Two-sided tests need fewer visitors
choices.why: They need more for the same improvement.

choices.text: One side would miss harm
choices.why: Right. Harm reads as 'no improvement' instead of as a warning.

choices.text: statsmodels only offers two-sided tests
choices.why: It offers both.

choices.text: One-sided tests are not valid for conversion rates
choices.why: They are valid; they answer a narrower question.

prompt: A company runs 100 tests in a year at a 5% significance level, and in 60 of them the change truly does nothing. About how many false wins should it expect among those 60?
Why is a test decided by one metric chosen before it starts?

choices.text: Picking the one that moved does not repeat
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11 measures how often.

choices.text: Dashboards can show one
choices.why: Dashboards show many; the rule is about deciding.

choices.text: Other metrics cannot be computed
choices.why: They are computed and reported as secondary.

choices.text: Statistics only works on conversion rates
choices.why: It works on many metrics; the issue is choosing after looking.

prompt: Match each property of a primary metric to its question.

pairs.right: if it moves, does the business care?
can the change move it within the test?
is it measured on the randomised unit?
does it arrive within the test's weeks?

right_distractors: is it the largest number on the dashboard?

prompt: Revenue per visitor is more relevant than conversion. Why is it a worse primary metric for Panela's checkout test?

choices.text: Revenue arrives months later
choices.why: First-order revenue arrives in the same visit; retention is the one that arrives late.

choices.text: It cannot be measured per visitor
choices.why: It can; it is just noisy.

choices.text: Revenue is a guardrail by definition
choices.why: It can be primary, secondary or a guardrail; here it is secondary.

choices.text: It is far noisier
choices.why: Right. It carries every box size and discount.

prompt: Panela randomises visitors. An analyst computes conversion per session, counting a visitor who came three times as three sessions. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Sessions are always fewer than visitors
choices.why: They are more, if anything.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as both groups are counted the same way
choices.why: Same counting does not fix observations that depend on each other.

choices.text: They stop being independent
choices.why: Right. Count on the unit that was randomised.

choices.text: Session data is not available
choices.why: It exists; sessions.csv holds it.

choices.text: A second primary metric
choices.why: A guardrail is not tested for improvement.

choices.text: A number that must not get worse
choices.why: Right. A clear harm stops the test.

choices.text: A limit on how long the test runs
choices.why: Duration comes from lesson 8's sample size.

choices.text: A metric hidden from the team so that nobody is tempted to look at it while the test runs
choices.why: Guardrails are watched openly, for harm.

prompt: A one-step checkout hides the delivery fee until the box arrives. Conversion rises. Which guardrail is most likely to catch the problem?

choices.text: Refund and complaint rate
choices.why: Right. The surprise fee becomes refunds and complaints.

choices.text: Page load time
choices.why: The page may load fast; the problem comes later.

choices.text: Average first-order value
choices.why: The order value may not change at all.

choices.text: Error rate on the payment step, which shows whether the new form breaks
choices.why: Nothing breaks technically.

prompt: The test ran its planned length and the result is inconclusive. What has the team learnt?

choices.text: Nothing; the test should be rerun until it gives an answer
choices.why: Rerunning until something appears is fishing.

choices.text: That the change does nothing at all
choices.why: It may do something smaller than the test could detect.

choices.text: That the significance level was too strict for a change of this size and should be relaxed
choices.why: Loosening it after the fact is choosing the criterion after seeing the data.

choices.text: That any effect is smaller than the planned 0.6 points
choices.why: Right. Enough to decide whether to keep it on other grounds.

prompt: Why must the success criterion be written before the test starts?

choices.text: Managers ask for it
choices.why: They may, but the reason is statistical honesty.

choices.text: The software needs it as input
choices.why: No software reads it; people do.

choices.text: Chosen afterwards, it only describes the data
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To save time later
choices.why: It saves arguments, but that is not why.

prompt: Put the parts of a test plan in the order this lesson builds them.
items: the hypothesis, with its size and reason
the primary metric and its unit

prompt: In an A/B test, the version that already exists is usually called the ___.
Panela tests a new recipe-recommendation panel on the menu page. Which primary metric fits a three-week test best?

choices.text: Customer retention after six months
choices.why: Most relevant, and it arrives far too late.

choices.text: Share of visitors who add a recipe to their box
choices.why: Right. Sensitive, attributable and timely, with a clear link to orders.

choices.text: Total revenue of the company in those three weeks, compared with the same weeks of last year
choices.why: That is a before-and-after, with the calendar mixed in.

choices.text: Number of page views of the menu
choices.why: Views can rise without anybody ordering more; it is not relevant enough.
